clue.text: One should keep records of ground rents

definitions.text: One should keep records of ground rents

parts.words: One should keep records of ground rents
parts.note: ground rents looks like money paid for land, but read it as rents (tears) in the ground, i.e. earthquakes, recorded by a scientist

explanation.surface: A landlord's clerk keeping the accounts of ground rents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground rents' is a property term, but here rents are rips: splits in the earth made by tremors.
explanation.definitionFit: A seismographer measures and records earthquakes, which tear the earth's crust.

clue.text: Identifying Lord's, for example, as favourite meeting-place

parts.note: stamping a mark on something identifies it
Lord's is a famous London cricket ground

explanation.surface: Picking out Lord's cricket ground as a favourite haunt.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground, home of the MCC.
explanation.definitionFit: One's stamping ground is a haunt often visited.

clue.text: Journey's end for Mrs Moore in raising support

indicators.note: raising, in a down clue, lifts the word so it reads upwards

parts.note: aid means help or support

explanation.surface: A traveller's destination in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Moore is a character in E M Forster's A Passage to India; 'raising' turns AID upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In Forster's novel Mrs Moore's passage takes her to this country.

clue.text: Imitation Dutch house-plant

parts.note: mock means imitation, fake
the House of Orange is the Dutch royal family

explanation.surface: A fake house-plant from Holland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House-plant' reads as one word, but it splits: Dutch house is the royal House of Orange, and plant is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Mock orange is a shrub, philadelphus, with fragrant white flowers.

clue.text: Held to have died shortly after attack of flu

indicators.note: after places the abbreviation for died behind the attack of flu

parts.note: grippe is an old word for influenza
d is the short form of died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Someone died soon after catching flu.
explanation.definitionFit: Gripped means clutched or grasped tightly.

clue.text: One can not recall having it

definitions.text: One can not recall having it

parts.words: One can not recall having it
parts.note: the condition takes away memory, so a sufferer cannot remember even suffering from it

explanation.definitionFit: The condition is a loss of memory.

clue.text: Hard fish to skin

parts.note: h is the pencil grading for hard
the ide is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Skinning a tough fish.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal's hide is its skin.

clue.text: Tackle mother over duty? What a performance!

indicators.note: over, in a down clue, puts mother above duty

parts.note: rig is gear or tackle
ma is mother
a role is one's part or duty

explanation.surface: Gear, mum, a job: what a palaver!
explanation.definitionFit: A rigmarole is a long, tedious fuss or procedure.

clue.text: Hanky-panky? There's 500. on the line!

parts.note: a monkey is British slang for five hundred pounds
a line of work is a business

explanation.surface: Five hundred pounds is at stake in some funny business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the line' suggests a bet at risk; the line is a line of trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkey business is mischief or trickery.

clue.text: Chester's first' in' increasing, dependence on horse, for example.

indicators.note: the first letter of Chester's goes into the word for increasing

parts.note: increasing is adding to, an addition

indicators.note: first tells us to take only the opening letter of Chester's

explanation.surface: Something about Chester's growing reliance on a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is slang for heroin, so dependence on horse is a drug habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Dependence on a drug such as heroin is a habit or craving.

clue.text: People in hiding lie, thus

parts.note: the idiom for keeping quiet and concealed is to lie in this way, so the clue completes the phrase

explanation.surface: Fugitives tell untruths, therefore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie' tempts as telling untruths; it is lying low, as in the slang phrase for staying hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase 'lie doggo' means stay still and hidden.

clue.text: Moon-crater made' by pilot initially a lot off course

indicators.note: initially means take only the first letter of pilot
a pilot off course wanders, so the letters of a lot are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pilot steering badly near a lunar crater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off course' rearranges A LOT into LATO, after P from pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato is a large named crater on the Moon's surface.

clue.text: Blight, found in overripe strawberries

indicators.note: found in says the letters sit within the words overripe strawberries

explanation.surface: Disease spotted on fruit that has gone too soft.
explanation.definitionFit: A blight is something harmful or troublesome, a nuisance.

clue.text: Rotten Row

definitions.meaning: a row is a line or tier, as of soldiers

explanation.walkthrough: Rotten Row is a famous riding track in London's Hyde Park, which hides the two separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank means smelly and offensive, and also a line of people such as a taxi queue.

clue.text: These jumpers always ride up!

parts.note: jumpers suggests sweaters creeping up, but these are soldiers who ride up in planes only to jump out

explanation.definitionFit: Airborne soldiers fly up in aircraft and descend by parachute.

clue.text: Mean sort of monotonous retirement, practically?

indicators.note: retirement is a going back, so the word is read in reverse
practically means almost, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: monotonous, tedious, is dragging

explanation.surface: A dull, nearly endless retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Practically' cuts DRAGGING to DRAGGIN, and 'retirement' turns it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A niggard is a miserly person who hates to spend.

clue.text: Left our sugar out while chattering:

indicators.note: out signals the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: Gossiping so much that the sugar was left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges L with OUR SUGAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A garrulous person talks too much.

clue.text: Gray's work is a short book in any case

indicators.note: in places the short book with its article inside the word any
short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: Some book by Gray is brief, whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Anatomy is the classic medical textbook by Henry Gray. 'In any case' reads as 'whatever happens', but 'any' is the case holding the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Gray's famous textbook describes the structure of the human body.

clue.text: Like a covered wagon, a sensation in outskirts of Gravesend?

indicators.note: in says the craze goes between the town's outer letters
outskirts of a town are its edges, so take the first and last letters of Gravesend

parts.note: a rage is a craze or sensation

explanation.surface: A Kent town's outskirts thrilled by a covered wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: Gravesend is a town in Kent; only its first and last letters, G and D, are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A wagon kept under cover in a shed has been housed or stored.

clue.text: Medical disorder that can recur

indicators.note: disorder signals that the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: An illness that keeps returning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medical disorder' reads as illness; 'disorder' rearranges MEDICAL. A recurring decimal repeats digits forever.
explanation.definitionFit: A decimal fraction such as 0.333 can repeat its digits without end.

clue.text: Top-of-the-table trophy, 'edged with gold?

indicators.note: edged with says the gold comes after, bordering the trophy

parts.note: a plate is a prize cup or dish in racing
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A league leader's cup with a golden rim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top-of-the-table' suggests a league leader, but it is a high flat land.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is a flat elevated tableland, the top of a table of rock.

clue.text: Girl in word-play can be prudish

indicators.note: in puts the girl inside the word-play

parts.note: a pun is a play on words
Rita is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl's jokes can be prim.
explanation.definitionFit: A puritan has strict, prim moral views.

clue.text: Work a star can put off

annotationWithheld.why: Work a star can put off (4): OPUS is a work, but no parse of 'a star can put off' gives OPUS or its pieces
annotationWithheld.clue: Work a star can put off

clue.text: Craggy rock causing injury

definitions.meaning: a steep rocky outcrop on a hillside
an injury's healed mark on the skin

explanation.surface: A rough crag that hurts climbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is both a cliff face of bare rock and the mark left by a wound.

clue.text: More than one spoke of daisies' outer rims'

definitions.text: More than one spoke of daisies' outer rims

parts.words: More than one spoke of daisies' outer rims
parts.note: the ray petals round a daisy's edge stand out like the spokes of a wheel, so these are many such spokes

explanation.surface: Petals radiating from the edges of daisies.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines running from a centre to the rim, like wheel spokes, are radial lines.

clue.text: P-peer standing on his head is so funny!

indicators.note: standing on his head in a down clue turns the word upside down, read upwards

parts.note: a stammered peer, a lord, with his first letter repeated

explanation.surface: A stuttering aristocrat doing a headstand is hilarious.
explanation.walkthrough: The stammer in 'P-peer' tells you to stammer the synonym: L-LORD, read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Droll means amusing in a quirky way.

clue.text: Pure water in the Lake District?

definitions.meaning: pure as in sheer, nothing more than
a lake, as in Grasmere or Windermere in the north of England

explanation.walkthrough: The Lake District is a region of north-west England whose lakes are often called meres.
explanation.definitionFit: Mere means simple or sheer, and is also an old word for a lake.

clue.text: Tearful mother turning in honour?

indicators.note: turning means the word in is reversed

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A mother weeping when given an award.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Niobe wept endlessly after her children were killed.
explanation.definitionFit: Niobe is the mythical mother who turned to stone while still weeping.

clue.text: They say a little fellow on the underground uses it for timekeeping

indicators.note: they say tells us the phrase is heard, not spelt

parts.words: a little fellow on the underground
parts.note: a gnome, a little man, on the metro, a city underground railway

explanation.surface: A small man on the Tube relies on something to keep time.
explanation.walkthrough: METRO GNOME, said aloud, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A musician's ticking device keeps a steady beat.

clue.text: High tars pushed under the bridge in emergencies?

definitions.text: pushed under the bridge in emergencies?

parts.note: high meat or game is strong-smelling
tars and salts are both slang for sailors

explanation.surface: Sailors drunk under a ship's bridge during a crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' suggests a ship, matching the sailors, but it is the bridge of the nose, under which the restorative is held for a fainting person.
explanation.definitionFit: A restorative held beneath the nose revives someone who has fainted.
